question: How does an MRI scanner create images of the body?

passages.title: How Does an MRI Machine Use Magnets to Create Medical Images?
passages.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses powerful magnets, radio waves, and computer processing to create detailed pictures of structures inside the human body. Unlike X-rays and computed tomography (CT) scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation. Instead, it takes advantage of the magnetic properties of hydrogen atoms, which are abundant in water and fat throughout the body. The central magnet inside an MRI machine creates a strong, stable magnetic field that influences the behavior of hydrogen nuclei in the body. Radio waves briefly disturb their alignment, and specialized receiver coils detect the signals they produce as they return toward their original state. A computer then processes these signals to construct detailed images of organs, muscles, bones, blood vessels, and other tissues. Understanding this process requires looking at how magnets interact with the body, how hydrogen atoms generate detectable signals, and how an MRI scanner turns those signals into medical images. Why MRI machines use powerful magnets The human body contains large amounts of hydrogen because water and many biological molecules contain hydrogen atoms. It describes how quickly the hydrogen nuclei lose their coordinated motion in the plane perpendicular to the main magnetic field. Although the nuclei initially precess in a relatively coordinated way after a radiofrequency pulse, their magnetic interactions with one another and small variations in their local magnetic environments cause them to gradually lose synchronization. As this coordination decreases, the detectable signal becomes weaker. T1 and T2 relaxation provide different kinds of information about tissue composition and molecular surroundings. MRI scanners use these differences to create images with varying contrast. A third concept, called T2-star (T2*), describes signal loss caused by both interactions between nuclei and variations in the magnetic field. These variations can result from imperfections in the scanner’s magnetic field or differences in the magnetic properties of nearby tissues. Together, these relaxation processes explain why different tissues produce different signal patterns even when they contain similar amounts of hydrogen. The scanner must also determine where that signal originated. MRI machines accomplish this using additional magnetic fields produced by components called gradient coils. These coils create small, controlled variations in the main magnetic field across the body. As a result, hydrogen nuclei at different locations experience slightly different magnetic field strengths. Because the Larmor frequency depends on magnetic field strength, hydrogen nuclei in different locations precess at slightly different frequencies. This allows the scanner to distinguish signals according to their positions. MRI uses three main types of spatial encoding. Slice selection identifies a particular section of the body. The scanner applies a magnetic field gradient while transmitting a radiofrequency pulse. Because the precession frequency varies with position, the pulse affects hydrogen nuclei within a selected frequency range, corresponding to a particular slice. Frequency encoding helps identify the position of signals along one direction within that slice. A magnetic field gradient causes hydrogen nuclei at different locations to produce signals at different frequencies. Phase encoding provides positional information along another direction. How computers turn magnetic signals into images The signals detected by MRI receiver coils are not initially recognizable pictures. They are measurements containing information about the strength, frequency, and timing of signals from different locations. The scanner organizes these measurements into a mathematical data space called k-space. K-space does not represent the body as a conventional picture. Instead, it contains spatial frequency information that a computer can use to reconstruct an image. How radio waves produce an MRI signal The main magnet establishes the magnetic environment, but radio waves are needed to generate the signal used for imaging. An MRI scanner contains radiofrequency coils that transmit carefully timed pulses of electromagnetic energy. These pulses are tuned to the Larmor frequency of hydrogen nuclei in the magnetic field. When a radiofrequency pulse reaches the body, it transfers energy to the hydrogen nuclei and changes the direction of the net magnetization. The magnetization is tipped away from its original alignment with the main magnetic field. The amount of tipping depends on the strength and duration of the radiofrequency pulse. A pulse can rotate the net magnetization by a particular angle, commonly 90 or 180 degrees, depending on the imaging sequence being used. Once the pulse ends, the hydrogen nuclei begin returning toward their equilibrium state. During this process, their changing magnetic behavior produces a signal that receiver coils can detect. This is the basis of the term magnetic resonance. The scanner does not directly photograph hydrogen atoms. Instead, it detects electromagnetic signals associated with changes in the collective

passages.text: MRI does not directly measure electrical activity in neurons. Instead, it detects changes in blood oxygenation that are indirectly associated with neural activity. Another specialized technique is diffusion-weighted imaging. It measures how the movement of water molecules affects the MRI signal. Water molecules move continuously through tissues. Their movement is restricted or influenced by the microscopic structure of surrounding cells and membranes. In certain medical conditions, these movement patterns change. Diffusion-weighted MRI is particularly useful for detecting acute ischemic stroke, in which reduced blood supply damages brain tissue. MRI can also examine blood vessels through magnetic resonance angiography, or MRA. Some MRA techniques use differences in blood movement to make vessels visible without requiring an injected contrast agent. Other techniques use contrast materials to improve vascular detail. These applications demonstrate how the same basic magnetic principles can support different kinds of medical information. Why MRI does not use X-ray radiation MRI differs from conventional X-ray imaging and CT scanning because it does not rely on ionizing radiation. X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves that can pass through the body and are absorbed to different degrees by different tissues. These are the images that doctors use for diagnostic purposes. MRIs were invented in the 1970s and have become an important diagnostic tool. In fact, an estimated 40 million MRIs happen each year in the U.S. MRIs provide qualitative information — pictures of the inside of the body. But what if an MRI could provide “quantitative” information in the form of measurements? This is the goal of a research effort here at NIST — to build toward quantitative MRI that provides data and measurements, not just pictures. Quantitative MRIs are currently used in clinical trials for medical therapy and in some clinical settings. Researchers conducting clinical trials on cancer treatments, for example, need to be able to measure patients’ tumors over time. They need to know that if a tumor is shrinking, it’s because the medication is working and not because of variances in the measurements given by different MRI machines examining individual participants. How MRI can reveal more than anatomical structures Although MRI is widely used to examine anatomy, its capabilities extend beyond producing pictures of organs and tissues. One important application is functional MRI, commonly called fMRI. This technique detects changes in blood oxygenation associated with brain activity. When a region of the brain becomes more active, its demand for oxygen increases. Blood flow to that region also changes, often delivering more oxygenated blood than the active tissue immediately needs. Oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin have different magnetic properties. These differences influence the MRI signal, allowing the scanner to detect changes associated with brain activity. The resulting technique is called the blood oxygen level-dependent, or BOLD, method. Functional MRI does not directly measure electrical activity in neurons. Instead, it detects changes in blood oxygenation that are indirectly associated with neural activity. The receiver coils collect signals generated by the hydrogen nuclei, and the computer processes the information into images. Patients are generally asked to remain still because movement can blur the images or produce artifacts that interfere with interpretation. Some examinations require a contrast agent, commonly a gadolinium-based substance, to make particular structures or abnormalities easier to see. These agents alter the magnetic relaxation behavior of nearby hydrogen nuclei, changing the resulting signal. Contrast is not necessary for every MRI examination. Its use depends on the medical question, the body part being examined, and the patient’s medical circumstances. The length of an examination varies according to the number and type of imaging sequences required. After scanning, a radiologist examines the images, looking for changes in anatomy, tissue characteristics, or blood flow that may help explain a patient’s symptoms or monitor a medical condition. What determines the quality of an MRI image Several factors influence how clearly an MRI machine can display internal structures. Magnetic field strength is one important factor. These magnets contain coils made from materials that, when cooled to extremely low temperatures, conduct electricity with virtually no electrical resistance. Once an electrical current is established in the coils, it can continue flowing with very little energy loss, maintaining a powerful magnetic field. The superconducting coils are housed in a specially designed cryogenic system that keeps them cold. This arrangement allows MRI machines to produce strong magnetic fields continuously without requiring enormous amounts of electrical power to maintain the current. How hydrogen nuclei respond to a magnetic field When a person enters an MRI scanner, the main magnetic field affects the hydrogen nuclei throughout the body. Protons can occupy two possible energy states in the presence of the magnetic field. One state has a magnetic orientation aligned with the field and a slightly lower energy. The other has an orientation opposed to the field and a slightly higher energy. There are slightly more protons in the lower-energy state than in the higher-energy state. But new technology is shrinking the MRI machine, and some machines can now travel to the patient. Thanks to recent advances, some MRI machines are small enough to fit in the back of a truck or to be brought into an ICU and plugged into a simple wall outlet, though they are not yet in widespread use. Known as low-field MRI, these machines have the potential to make health care much more accessible to people who don’t have a hospital nearby. One of the challenges with low-field MRI is the quality of the images, but we’re also studying how to use AI to improve these images and demonstrate the clinical utility of these systems. The goal of this work is to make low-field MRIs more useful as they become more common. More research is needed to make sure these machines take the most accurate possible measurements. But measurement is what NIST does. We’ll keep learning more about these new developments in MRI technology — so you can be your healthiest.

Given that the protons are affected by fields from other atoms to which they are bonded, it is possible to separate responses from hydrogen in specific compounds. To perform a study, the person is positioned within an MRI scanner that forms a strong magnetic field around the area to be imaged. First, energy from an oscillating magnetic field is temporarily applied to the patient at the appropriate resonance frequency. Scanning with X and Y gradient coils causes a selected region of the patient to experience the exact magnetic field required for the energy to be absorbed. The atoms are excited by a RF pulse and the resultant signal is measured by one or more receiving coils. The RF signal may be processed to deduce position information by looking at the changes in RF level and phase caused by varying the local magnetic field using gradient coils. To create a T1-weighted image, magnetization is allowed to recover before measuring the MR signal by changing the repetition time (TR). This image weighting is useful for assessing the cerebral cortex, identifying fatty tissue, characterizing focal liver lesions, and in general, obtaining morphological information, as well as for post-contrast imaging. To create a T2-weighted image, magnetization is allowed to decay before measuring the MR signal by changing the echo time (TE). This image weighting is useful for detecting edema and inflammation, revealing white matter lesions, and assessing zonal anatomy in the prostate and uterus. The information from MRI scans comes in the form of image contrasts based on differences in the rate of relaxation of nuclear spins following their perturbation by an oscillating magnetic field (in the form of radiofrequency pulses through the sample).[24] The relaxation rates are a measure of the time it takes for a signal to decay back to an equilibrium state from either the longitudinal or transverse plane. Using a mathematical operation called the Fourier transform, the scanner converts the collected data into a spatial representation of the body’s internal structures. The resulting image is made up of pixels in two-dimensional scans or voxels in three-dimensional scans. Each pixel or voxel represents the signal characteristics of a small region of tissue. The brightness of each region depends on several factors, including hydrogen content, T1 and T2 relaxation times, magnetic field strength, and the timing and design of the imaging sequence. This explains why the same tissue can appear bright in one MRI image and dark in another. The scanner can adjust its sequence to emphasize particular tissue characteristics. The computer can also combine information from multiple slices to produce detailed three-dimensional representations of organs and other structures. Why different tissues appear differently on MRI scans One of MRI’s greatest advantages is its ability to distinguish between soft tissues that may look similar on other imaging tests. Mechanisms of contrast enhancement in magnetic resonance imaging Because tumors and inflamed tissues tend to have leaky blood vessels that accumulate more contrast agent than healthy tissue, they “light up” after gadolinium injection. This enhancement helps radiologists distinguish a benign cyst (which does not enhance) from a solid tumor (which often does), or identify areas of active inflammation in conditions like multiple sclerosis. Gadolinium-based agents are injected intravenously and are cleared by the kidneys, usually within hours. Functional MRI and Brain Activity One of the more striking applications of MRI does not image anatomy at all. Functional MRI, or fMRI, maps brain activity by detecting changes in blood oxygenation. When a region of the brain becomes more active, local blood flow increases and delivers more oxygenated hemoglobin than the tissue is consuming. Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic and disturbs the local magnetic field, while oxyhemoglobin is not. So when a brain area “lights up” with activity, the local ratio shifts toward oxyhemoglobin, reducing magnetic field disturbances and producing a slightly stronger MRI signal.7PubMed Central. For the tipping to work correctly, this radio wave must have a particular frequency, which depends on the basic properties of the protons. This frequency matching is the “resonance” in MRI. If you’ve ever heard the phrase “on the same wavelength,” this is a similar concept! After the radiofrequency pulse passes through the body, the protons’ little magnets move back into their original positions. As the protons “relax” back into these positions, they release electromagnetic signals that the MRI machine “sees.” These signals contain information about the protons’ position in the body as well as their environment (such as healthy tissue or tumors). We’re not done yet, though. The MRI machine needs to repeat the process of firing radiofrequency pulses many times to build up images. Each time, the machine turns on spatially varying magnetic fields (known as magnetic field gradients) to encode the location of protons within the MRI signal. The spatial information is critical for creating a 3D image. When the scan is finished, computers combine information from all the signals to create images of the body.
